details:
**Golden plates and the angel Moroni**
Smith said the angel Moroni led him to a set of golden plates buried in the Hill Cumorah near Manchester, New York. He translated them as the Book of Mormon, published in 1830, and the plates appear in nearly every question about him.

**Urim and Thummim (seer stones)**
Seer stones that Smith said he used to translate the golden plates; the name is borrowed from the priestly objects in the Hebrew Bible. In 2015 the LDS Church released the first photographs of a seer stone attributed to him.

**Reformed Egyptian**
The script in which, according to Smith, the golden plates were written. He presented the Book of Mormon as a translation of this otherwise unknown language.

**Three Witnesses**
Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris, who testified that an angel showed them the golden plates. Their statement is printed in most editions of the Book of Mormon. Cowdery was also Smith's main scribe, and the two said John the Baptist appeared to them and baptized them.

**Death at Carthage Jail**
In June 1844, while held in jail in Carthage, Illinois, Smith and his brother Hyrum were shot and killed by an armed mob. Hostility toward him had grown in nearby Nauvoo, including over his destruction of a critical newspaper and rumors of polygamy.

**Nauvoo, Illinois**
The city Smith's followers built on the Mississippi River after they were expelled from Missouri in 1838–1839. It became the center of the movement and the place where Smith publicly denied charges of polygamy.

**Word of Wisdom**
A revelation by Smith, part of the Doctrine and Covenants, that warns against alcohol ("strong drinks"), tobacco, and "hot drinks" (understood as coffee and tea). It is the basis of Latter-day Saint dietary rules.

**Lost 116 pages**
Martin Harris borrowed and lost the first 116 manuscript pages of Smith's translation, known as the Book of Lehi. Smith said God punished him and did not have him retranslate that section, replacing it with a different account from the small plates of Nephi.

**Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price**
Two Latter-day Saint scriptures alongside the Bible and Book of Mormon. Doctrine and Covenants collects Smith's revelations, including instructions on baptism for the dead, while the Pearl of Great Price contains his translation of part of Matthew and his Articles of Faith, the second of which rejects inherited original sin.

**First Vision (Sacred Grove)**
Smith's account of seeing God the Father and Jesus Christ while praying in a grove of trees near his home in upstate New York around 1820. He described it in sources including the 1842 Wentworth Letter.

**Jackson County, Missouri (Zion)**
Smith declared Jackson County, Missouri, to be the site of Zion, the New Jerusalem, and visited it with Oliver Cowdery and others. The Latter-day Saints were later driven out of the county and then out of Missouri.

**King Follett discourse**
A sermon Smith gave in 1844 at the funeral of church member King Follett. It taught exaltation, the controversial idea that God was once a man and that humans can become gods.

**Endowment, Quorum of the Twelve, and Council of Fifty**
Smith created the endowment, a temple ceremony that reenacts the Fall of Adam and Eve and whose oaths resemble Masonic ones. He also organized the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and the secret Council of Fifty.

**James Strang**
One of several men who claimed to succeed Smith after his death. Strang led his followers to Beaver Island in Lake Michigan and was crowned "King of the Kingdom of God," while most Latter-day Saints followed Brigham Young to Utah.

**Salamander Letter**
A forged letter attributed to Martin Harris, created by Mark Hofmann in the 1980s. In its version of the story of the golden plates, a white salamander that turned into a spirit took the place of the angel Moroni. Hofmann later killed two people with bombs to avoid exposure and was convicted of murder.
